lesson.text: Quick memory: in grade 6, how does a computer learn to tell cats from rabbits? (From many examples that people have labelled.) Today: how machine learning finds patterns, and how bias gets in.
In machine learning, people do not write every rule. They give a program training data: many examples with the right answers, called labels. The program finds a pattern in them: a model.
Worked example: each animal is measured two ways. A new animal is placed among the examples. The simplest model gives it the label of its nearest example: here, rabbit.
Then the model is tested on examples it has never seen. If it labels 45 of 50 right, its accuracy is 90%. A model is never right every time.
Bias gets in through the data. A face model trained mostly on light-skinned faces makes more mistakes on darker skin; a voice model trained on few accents may not understand others.
What AI can do: find patterns in huge amounts of data, translate, turn speech into words, suggest the next word. What it cannot do: understand as a person does, know what is true, or care.
Good habits: check AI's answers in trusted sources, as chatbots can sound sure and still be wrong. Never give it private details, and say when you used it. People are responsible for what AI does.
Try it in the world: sort 20 leaves into two kinds by length and width. Then measure a new leaf: which leaf is it nearest to? Next: cyber security.

exercises.hint: Think about what the program learns from.
exercises.explain: Training data is many examples, each labelled with the right answer, so the program can find a pattern.

exercises.prompt: A machine learning model is right every time.
exercises.explain: False: a model makes mistakes; that is why it is tested and checked.

exercises.prompt: Which group does the new animal's nearest example belong to?
exercises.hint: Find the example closest to the ? and look at its shape.
exercises.explain: The ringed nearest example is a triangle, a rabbit, so the model says rabbit.

exercises.prompt: A model gets 9 of 10 test examples right. What is its accuracy as a percentage?
exercises.hint: Write it as a fraction of 10, then make it out of 100.

items: find patterns in lots of data
know for sure what is true
exercises.hint: Is it finding a pattern, or is it a feeling or knowing?
exercises.explain: AI finds patterns, translates and predicts words; it does not care or know for sure what is true.

exercises.prompt: A model labels 42 of 50 new photos right. What is its accuracy as a percentage?
A model learned only from photos of dogs taken in daylight. What might go wrong?
choices: it may fail on dogs in the dark
it will be better at night
it will learn to see cats too
exercises.hint: A model only knows what was in its examples.
exercises.explain: It never saw a dark photo, so it may not recognise a dog at night: its data was biased towards daylight.

exercises.prompt: Bias in a model can come from its training data.
exercises.hint: Where does a model get its pattern from?
exercises.explain: True: if some people or things are missing from the data, the model works worse for them.

exercises.prompt: Match each word to its meaning.
exercises.hint: Follow the order: learn, then check.
exercises.explain: Training data teaches, the model is what was learned, test data checks it and accuracy is its score.

exercises.prompt: Put the steps of machine learning in order.
exercises.hint: What must exist before anything is learned?
exercises.explain: Collect, label, train, test on new examples, then use it and keep checking.

exercises.prompt: The new one's 3 nearest examples are ringed. What does a vote of the 3 say?
exercises.hint: Count the shapes among the ringed examples.
exercises.explain: Of the 3 nearest, 2 are rabbits and 1 is a cat, so the vote says rabbit.

exercises.prompt: Training photos: 180 cats and 20 rabbits. What percentage are rabbits?
A chatbot gives a confident answer with a date in it. What should you do?
choices: check it in a trusted source
ask the chatbot if it is sure
exercises.hint: Can sounding sure make an answer true?
exercises.explain: Chatbots can be wrong while sounding sure, so check facts in a trusted book or site.

exercises.prompt: Adding more varied training examples can reduce bias.
exercises.hint: Bias comes from what is missing from the data.
exercises.explain: True: examples of every kind help the model work well for everyone.

exercises.prompt: A voice helper for everyone: fair or biased training data?
exercises.hint: Would everyone who uses it be in the data?
exercises.explain: Data with all ages, accents and ways of speaking is fair; data with one kind of voice is biased.

exercises.prompt: Model A gets 88 of 100 right; model B gets 45 of 50. How many percentage points better is B?
